source.title: Can Large Language Models Truly Understand Prompts? A Case Study with Negated Prompts
source.authors: Joel Jang; Seonghyeon Ye; Minjoon Seo

record.tranche_reason: The study measures downstream task performance across model scales and reports inverse scaling on negated prompts, challenging the claim that downstream performance improves predictably with scale in those conditions.
record.gate_note: The paper evaluates task performance on original and manually negated prompts. It states that larger models perform worse on negated prompts and provides plots by dataset and model scale. Numeric plot values are not stated in the text. The average-score comparison in Figure 3 and the fine-tuning trade-off are not separately recorded as rows because they combine original and negated prompt performance rather than isolate the scaling result.
record.test_reason: The study evaluates zero-shot downstream task accuracy across model sizes (OPT 125M–66B, GPT-3 Ada–Davinci, InstructGPT, T0). It reports that accuracy on negated prompts falls with scale. This is a direct result against V6's claim that downstream performance improves with scale.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. Accuracy on negated prompts gets worse with scale (inverse scaling) for pretrained and instruction-tuned models. Original/negated averages stay at ~50%. ICL helps only in some settings. Fine-tuning on negated prompts trades away original-prompt accuracy, a zero-sum outcome. The best method still trails 13-year-old humans by about 31.3%.
record.recipe_differences: Measures zero-shot downstream task performance under original and negated prompts across model sizes, rather than held-out pretraining loss against parameters, tokens, or compute.
record.method_sensitivity: Prompt polarity changes the reported scaling trend: original-prompt performance improves with size, while negated-prompt performance worsens. The study also reports task-dependent results for its other evaluation settings.
record.code_released: The paper says code and datasets are provided at a link, but no URL is present in the supplied text.
record.problems: The numeric results for the scale comparisons are presented in figures and not specified in the text; uncertainty estimates are not stated. The GPT-3 scale figure displays four sizes, while the OPT appendix displays eight.
record.rows_left_out: Figure 3 and Figures 5–13 also show comparisons among ICL, fine-tuning, instruction-following models, and humans. Those comparisons were not extracted as additional rows because the reported average combines original and negated prompt performance and does not isolate the scaling result. Fine-tuning results are also a separately induced training setting.

untested.parts: Whether downstream performance is predictable from pretraining loss; any fitted functional form of downstream performance against scale.
Not tested: no pretraining loss is measured.
Not tested: no fits or extrapolation.
Not tested: no other modalities or training regimes as scaling-law settings.
Not tested: no fitting choices or exponents.

missing.what: OPT original-prompt accuracy across sizes. This is the counterpart to r2 and is needed to confirm that positive scaling holds in the same OPT sweep.
Average of original and negated prompt accuracy stays flat at ~50% across scale for GPT-3 and OPT. Gains on the original prompts are offset by losses on the negated prompts.
Negated-prompt accuracy of OPT fine-tuned on negated prompts at 125M, 350M and 1.3B. The abstract claims these models also worsen with scale, but no row records it.

record.verdict_notes: All scale results are figure-only, with no numbers in the text and no uncertainty. There are 300 instances per dataset, and human evaluation covers only 3 tasks. The authors frame the negated-prompt result as an inverse scaling law, so it is the direction of improvement, not merely its predictability, that fails under negation. The original-prompt support (r3) is weak because the text cites prior work for it.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not measure held-out pretraining cross-entropy loss against parameter count, training tokens, or compute.
The study does not fit power laws on smaller runs or test predictions on larger runs.
The study does not compare parameter and token allocations at fixed compute.
The study does not compare architecture details at fixed parameter count.
The study does not test other modalities, repeated data, fine-tuning or transfer as scaling-law settings.
The study tests zero-shot task performance across model sizes on original and negated prompts, but does not test whether downstream performance is predictable from pretraining loss.
The study does not investigate scaling-law fit choices, exponents, compute-optimal allocation, or curvature in loss-versus-scale curves.
